title: Rapamycin coated selenium nanoparticles relieve oxidative senescence of vascular endothelium by mitophagy

sections.abstract: Rapamycin (RPM) extends longevity in various species and combats vascular senescence related diseases. Selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs) have attracted attention as a potential therapy for cardiovascular diseases due to their excellent antioxidant and drug-carrying capacity. However, RPM coated SeNPs (RPM-SeNPs) have not been reported and their potential for preventing endothelial oxidative senescence remains unclear. In the present study, RPM-SeNPs were generated by selenite and RPM with ascorbic acid reduction. Stability and dispersity of SeNPs were increased by coating with RPM, resulting in an average diameter of 67.51 ± 2.07 nm with a RPM:Se molar ratio of 1:120. Notably, RPM-SeNPs exhibited ameliorative effects on oxidative endothelial senescence in mouse aortas or MAECs induced by paraquat or hydrogen peroxide, respectively. There were evidenced by decreased SA-β-gal activity, lower SASP levels, and decreased endothelial dysfunction. Mechanically, RPM-SeNPs reduced oxidative stress in endothelial cells by upregulating GPX4, particularly mitochondrial GPX4 (mtGPX4) that mitigated of ROS and relieved mitochondria dysfunction. By downregulating the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, RPM-SeNPs inhibited ULK1 phosphorylation at Ser757, subsequently leading to the activation of mitophagy and the reversal of mitochondrial dysfunction, including mitochondrial membrane potential collapse and ATP deficiency. Thus, these results suggest that RPM-SeNPs rescue endothelial cells from oxidative stress induced senescence by upregulating mtGPX4 and activating mitophagy. These results provide insight into the mechanisms of functionalizing SeNPs for potentially treating senescence-related diseases.
sections.introduction:
Vascular endothelial cell senescence plays a key role in aging-related cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) such as atherosclerosis, hypertension and diabetes [ 1 ]. This affects endothelial function in terms of vascular permeability, vasoconstriction, thrombosis and inflammation [ 1 ]. Cell senescence may be triggered by endogenous and exogenous stresses, with oxidative stress playing a key role in inducing senescence [ 2 ]. Oxidative stress is particularly common in vascular endothelial cells (VECs) due to the strategic location of VECs lining the inner surface of blood vessels [ 3 ]. Typically, senescent VECs are characterized by flattened and enlarged morphology, along with senescence-associated beta-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activation, senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) components secretion, autophagy dysfunction, and cell cycle arrest, which eventually lead to the onset of endothelial dysfunction [ 4 ].

Rapamycin (RPM) is an inhibitor of mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) that inhibits cell senescence and increases longevity in a range of organisms from yeast to mammals [ [5] , [6] , [7] , [8] ]. RPM improves physiological parameters in the cardiovascular [ 9 ], nervous [ 10 ], and integumentary systems [ 11 , 12 ], and is a prophylactic anti-aging drug [ 13 ]. RPM exerts targeted protection against vascular aging by mitigating key pathological features, including endothelial dysfunction, VSMCs phenotypic switching, vascular inflammation, and plaque instability [ 14 , 15 ]. Notably, advances in nano-encapsulation now enable targeted delivery of RPM to inflamed vasculature, enhancing its therapeutic activity in preclinical models of atherosclerosis while minimizing systemic side effects [ 16 ]. RPM exerts its effects predominantly by inhibiting mTOR signaling, thereby modulating autophagy, metabolic regulation, cell proliferation and growth [ 17 ]. Autophagy is largely viewed as a self-limiting, protective and anti-senescence process that facilitates the degradation of surplus proteins and dysfunctional organelles [ 18 ]. Consistent with this notion, activation of autophagy by mTOR inhibition has been implicated in the suppression of cellular senescence [ 19 , 20 ] . Notably, impairment of mitochondrial turnover by autophagy (i.e. mitophagy) leads to accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria. This is characterized by hallmarks such as ROS generation, ATP production and mitochondrial membrane potential [ 21 , 22 ]. By removing damaged mitochondria, mitophagy diminishes the release of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) that can serve as a damage-associated molecular pattern and trigger inflammatory responses in senescent cells [ 23 , 24 ]. RPM enhances mitophagy by inhibiting phosphorylation of PI3K/Akt/mTOR/ULK1 (Ser757) or promoting phosphorylation of AMPK/ULK1 (Ser555), which both stimulate removal of dysfunctional mitochondria to restore cellular homeostasis [ 25 , 26 ]. Although RPM offers therapeutic potential for aging-related diseases, its clinical application is limited by the challenge of determining the minimal effective dose [ 27 ]. Current studies have focusd on the developing of biomaterial-based nanoparticles and hydrogels that can deliver RPM in a prolonged and stabilized manner [ [28] , [29] , [30] , [31] ].

Selenium (Se) is a micronutrient essential for human health by coordinating immune responses, thyroid hormone metabolism, reproduction, and defenses against oxidative damage [ 32 ]. The biological activity of Se is of interest because it is both essential and toxic to humans depending on the species. The chemical speciation of Se includes various organic and inorganic Se compounds, in which Se can exist in different redox states (Se−2, Se+2, Se+4 and Se+6). Whereas Se exists in zero-valence state (Se0) in selenium nanoparticles (SeNPs), which possess excellent bio-reactivity that can be oxidized or reduced after sustained releasing in body. Thus, SeNPs have been believed to not only provide Se nutritional supplement but also significantly reduce the potential risk of toxicity of other Se species [ [33] , [34] , [35] ]. In recent years, accumulating literatures have reported that SeNPs can serve as a broad deliverable nanoscale platform for many bioactive molecules and drugs after functionalization [ 33 , 36 , 37 ]. Up to now, various methods have been reported for SeNPs preparation including physical approaches such as pulsed laser ablation and microwave, chemical reduction of inorganic Se, and biosynthesis strategies by utilizing plant extracts or microbes [ 35 , 38 , 39 ]. Based on the synergy effect of Se and bioactive molecules coated, a variety of decorated SeNPs have been designed and evidenced that exhibited anti-oxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-tumor bioactivities, demonstrating therapeutic potential for cardiovascular diseases, infectious diseases, diabetes, colitis, and cancer [ [40] , [41] , [42] , [43] , [44] ]. SeNPs act mechanistically to release Se into cells, which is then metabolized into selenocysteine that serves to increase selenoprotein bioactivity [ 45 ]. Among the 25 human selenoproteins, glutathione peroxidases (GPXs) are a family of eight antioxidant enzymes that utilize reduced glutathione (GSH) to catalyze the reduction of reactive oxygen species such as H 2 O 2 and lipid peroxides, thereby maintaining redox homeostasis [ 46 ]. GPX4 is a versatile selenoenzyme that localizes to the cytosol (cGPX4), mitochondria and nucleus, with mitochondrial GPX4 (mtGPX4) serving as an important defense of mitochondrial membranes from the high levels of ROS found in this organelle [ 47 ]. Besides, GPX4 is involved in autophagy, and its deficiency causes irreversible oxidation of Atg3/Atg7, suppressing mitophagy [ 48 ]. Functionalized SeNPs can defend against the aging process by targeting oxidative stress [ 36 , 49 ], but it remains unclear whether combining SeNPs with RPM may effectively protect against vascular oxidative senescence via the activation of mitophagy.

In the present study, RPM-SeNPs were synthesized and investigated for effects on oxidative stress-induced endothelial senescence in vivo and in vitro . RPM-SeNPs were found to relieve oxidative stress-induced senescence in mouse aortas and mouse aortic endothelial cells (MAECs). RPM-SeNPs lowered levels of SA-β-gal activity and SASP to alleviate endothelial dysfunction. Mitochondrial homeostasis was improved by upregulation of mtGPX4 as a mechanism to mitigate damage from oxidative stress, thereby maintaining mitophagy that effectively removed dysfunctional mitochondria. Overall, these results provide new insights into the anti-aging effects exerted by RPM-SeNPs as a modality that may be utilized to reduce oxidative endothelium senescence-related CVDs.
sections.methods:
SeNPs and RPM-SeNPs were prepared according to our previous study with minor modifications. Briefly, 500 μL of sodium selenite solution (10 mM; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was added into 10 mL of distilled water, containing poloxamer 407 (0.01 %; Meilun, Dalian, China) or sodium selenite solution containing poloxamer 407 and RPM (2.5 mM; MCE, Princeton, NJ, USA). Ascorbic acid solution (500 μL at 40 mM; Aladdin, Shanghai, China) was added dropwise into the mixture and the reactions were kept for 12 h at 4 °C. The solution was dialyzed against distilled water for 24 h. Additionally, coumarin-6 (5 μg/mL; C6, Aladdin, Shanghai, China) was added to label RPM-SeNPs and SeNPs (RPM-SeNPs&C6 and SeNPs&C6) for the tracing investigation.

RPM-SeNPs and SeNPs were characterized using a Field Emission Electron Microscope (TEM; JEM 2100F; JEOL, Showima City, Tokyo, Japan), an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS; K-Alpha; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), a UV–Vis spectrophotometer (Cary 4000; Agilent, Santa Clara, CA, USA), and a fourier transform infrared spectrometer (FTIR; Nicolet™ iS™ 10; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Besides, the average particle diameter, size distribution, polydispersity index (PDI) and Zeta potential of RPM-SeNPs and SeNPs were measured using Malvern Zetasizer (Nano ZS; Malvern Instruments, Great Malvern. UK).

All animal protocols were approved by accordance with the Animal Care and Ethics Committee of Jinan University (No. 20220305-18). Male C57BL/6J mice (6-weeks-old) were obtained from the Experimental Animal Center of Southern Medical University (Guangzhou, China) and housed in a temperature-controlled room (22 ± 1 °C) with a 12 h light/dark cycle at the Institute of Laboratory Animal Science, Jinan University. The animals were maintained with ad libitum access to water and food throughout the experiment. Mice were divided into 5 groups (n = 10 per group) and received intraperitoneal an injection of PBS (control) or paraquat (PQ; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). The groups included PQ at 7 mg/kg, daily for 1 week; PQ + RPM-SeNPs; PQ + RPM and PQ + SeNPs. The PQ + RPM-SeNPs and PQ + RPM and PQ + SeNPs groups were then intravenously injected with either PBS, RPM-SeNPs (0.08 mg Se/kg) SeNPs (0.08 mg Se/kg) or RPM (0.05 mg/kg) with the with the same loaded concentration every other day for 1 week. Body weights were measured daily and mice were euthanized for the collection of aortas.

Mouse aortic endothelial cells (MAECs; ATCC) and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs; ATCC) were cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium (DMEM; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS; Royacel, Lanzhou, China) and 1 % penicillin/streptomycin (GBCBIO, Guangzhou, China) at 37 °C in a 5 % CO 2 incubator (Forma™ II; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). MAECs were pre-treated with H 2 O 2 (200 mM, 4 h; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) for inducing oxidative senescence, followed by treatment with RPM-SeNPs (2 μM Se), SeNPs (2 μM Se) and RPM (100 nM) for 24 h.

The Senescence β-Galactosidase Staining Kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) was used to detect senescent endothelial cells and aortic cells following the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, aortas and cells were fixed, washed in PBS, and incubated with the staining solution overnight at 37 °C. Images of cells and aortas were captured using EVOS EL Auto Imaging System.

The aorta tissues, treated cells, or the mitochondria isolated using the mitochondrial isolation kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) were lysed on ice with radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) containing a protease inhibitor cocktail (0.1 %; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). The lysate supernatants were then collected and the protein concentrations were determined by Bradford protein assay (Yeasen, Shanghai, China). After equalization with loading buffer (Yeasen, Shanghai, China), the samples were boiled, separated by SDS-PAGE, and transferred to PVFD membranes (0.22 μm; Millipore, Burlington, MA, USA). After blocking in 5 % skim milk (GBCBIO, Guangzhou, China), the membranes were incubated with the indicated primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight followed by the Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG (H + L) HRP (1:3000; Affinity, Changzhou, China) at room temperature for 1 h. Protein bands were visualized using electrochemiluminescence assay kits (Yeasen, Shanghai, China) and Tanon 5200 system (Shanghai, China).

Primary antibodies included anti-p21 (Affinity), anti-IL-1β (Affinity), anti-p53 Affinity), anti-CDKN2A/p16INK4a (Affinity), anti-SQSTM1/p62 (Affinity), anti-GPX1 (Affinity), anti-VDAC1 (Affinity), anti-Beclin1 (Affinity), anti-Actin (Affinity), anti-GPX4 (ABclonal, Wuhan, China), anti-LC3B (ABclonal), anti-mTOR (ABclonal), anti- p -mTOR (Ser2448, ABclonal), anti-PI3K (ABclonal) and anti-p-PI3K (Y467/Y464/Y199, ABclonal), anti-ULK1 (MCE), anti- p -ULK1 (Ser757, MCE), anti-Akt (Cell Signaling Technology), and anti- p -Akt (Ser473, Cell Signaling Technology), and the dilutions are 1:1000.

Total RNA was extracted using Molpure® Cell/Tissue Total RNA Kit (Yeasen, Shanghai, China) following the manufacturer's instructions. Complementary DNA (cDNA) was reverse transcribed from a total of 1 μg RNA using Hifair® III 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis SuperMix (Yeasen, Shanghai, China). RT-qPCR was performed in triplicate using 2X Realstar Fast SYBR qPCR Mix (Genstar, Beijing, China) and CFX96 Touch Real-Time PCR detection System (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA) with the following parameters: 95 °C for 5 min, 40 cycles at 95 °C for 10 s, and 55 °C for 30 s. The mRNA levels of the target genes were normalized to the Actin levels and quantified by the 2 −ΔΔCt method. Primers listed in Table S1 were synthesized from Sangon Biotech Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China).

Aorta tissues and treated cells were lysed with RIPA buffer containing a protease inhibitor cocktail (0.1 %). The supernatants of lysates were then collected for the detection of MDA, GSH levels and GPX activity using assay kits (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, Nanjing, China) following the manufacturer's instructions.

Aortic sections were blocked with 5 % goat serum (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) and incubated with indicated primary antibodies at 4 °C overnight followed by incubation with goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (Alexa Fluor® 647; 1:500; Abcam, Shanghai, China). Sections were then counterstained with DAPI (1 μg/mL; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), sealed, and imaged by EVOS® FL Auto Imaging System.

MAECs were seeded onto poly- l -lysine-coated (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) coverslips and treated as above. Cells were fixed, permeabilized with 0.1 % Triton™ X-100, blocked with 1 % BSA (GBCBIO, Guangzhou, China), and incubated with indicated primary antibodies followed by goat anti-rabbit IgG H&L (Alexa Fluor® 647, 1:500; Abcam, Shanghai, China). After counterstaining with DAPI and sealing, images were captured using a confocal laser scanning microscope (FV3000; Olympus, Shinjuku City, Tokyo, Japan).

To visualize oxidized mitochondria, cells were treated as described above and incubated with MitoTracker® Red CM-H2XRos (Yeasen, Shanghai, China), and mitophagy visualization of treated cells was performed by incubation with MitoTracker® Red CMXRos (Yeasen, Shanghai, Chin), LysoTracker Green DND-26 (Yeasen, Shanghai, China) and Hoechst 33258 (Beyotime, Shanghai, China), followed by immunofluorescence procedure.

MAECs were seeded on confocal dishes for imaging and 6-well-plates, cells incubated with JC-1 (2 mM; MCE) for detecting mitochondrial membrane potential, CM-H 2 DCF-DA (5 μM; Beyotime, Shanghai, China) for detecting intracellular ROS, or MitoSOX Red (5 μM; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) for detecting mitochondrial ROS (mtROS). Representative images were obtained by using a confocal laser scanning microscope (FV3000; Olympus, Shinjuku City, Tokyo, Japan), and mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) was analyzed by using Image J software (version 1.46r; National Institutes of Health). Meanwhile, MAECs were harvested and analyzed by flow cytometry (NovoCyte®; Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA).

The treated MAECs were lysed and ATP content was measured using a firefly luciferase-based ATP assay kit (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) following the manufacturer's instructions. The luminescence intensity was measured using Synergy™ H1M.

Graphing and statistical analyses were performed using Origin 2025b (OriginLab, Northampton, MA, USA). Data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistically significant differences between two groups or more than two groups were calculated by unpaired Student's t-test or by one way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey's honestly significant difference (HSD) post-hoc test. Statistical differences were considered as a p -value of <0.05.

RPM-SeNPs and SeNPs were prepared, and particle size and morphology determined by TEM and Zetasizer. The TEM observations revealed that RPM-SeNPs presented as uniformly dispersed spherical nanoparticles, while bare SeNPs tended to aggregate ( Fig. 1 A, Fig. S1I ). Dynamic light scattering analysis showed that RPM-SeNPs exhibited a narrower size distribution (39–251 nm vs. 50–630 nm; Fig. 1 B), smaller average particle size (67.51 ± 2.07 nm vs. 212.33 ± 14.32 nm; Fig. 1 C), and improved suspension transparency ( Fig. 1 B) compared to bare SeNPs. RPM-SeNPs showed a significantly lower PDI (0.05 ± 0.01 vs. 0.34 ± 0.04; Fig. 1 D) than bare SeNPs, and indicated that the size distribution uniformity was improved. Additionally, the zeta potential of RPM-SeNPs was significantly more negative than that of bare SeNPs (−19.57 ± 1.49 mV vs. −5.42 ± 0.72 mV, Fig. S1A–C ). To verify the coating of RPM onto SeNPs, EDS, UV–Vis spectrophotometry, and FTIR spectroscopy were conducted. Surface elemental composition analysis by EDS detected a mass radio of nitrogen (0.74 %) in RPM-SeNPs, confirming the presence of RPM as the sole nitrogen source ( Fig. 1 E and F). UV–Vis spectral analysis showed that RPM and SeNPs exhibited a single absorption peak at 210 nm and 266 nm, respectively, while RPM-SeNPs presented dual absorption peaks at 206 nm and 260 nm due to the superposition of two components ( Fig. 1 G). The FTIR analysis of RPM-SeNPs revealed a shift of the carbonyl peak from 1720 cm −1 to 1724 cm −1 and a broadened O–H/N–H stretching band at 3424 cm −1 ( Fig. 1 H). The loading rate of RPM on RPM-SeNPs was determined by UV–Vis spectroscopy at 210 nm ( Fig. S1D ). RPM concentration in RPM-SeNPs was 24.7 ± 0.5 μM prior to dialysis, but reduced to 4.1 ± 0.3 μM after dialysis ( Fig. 1 I). The calculated loading efficiency was 16.57 ± 0.99 %, corresponding to an approximate molar ratio of RPM to SeNPs of 1:120. In vitro release studies were carried out under simulated physiological (pH 7.4) and intralysosomal (pH 5.5) conditions, and RPM-SeNPs exhibit a more efficient release efficiency of RPM at pH 5.5 than at pH 7.4 ( Fig. S1F ). Moreover, RPM-SeNPs remained stable for 4 weeks, as evidenced by consistent average size ( Fig. 1 J), size distribution ( Fig. S1G ), PDI ( Fig. 1 K), and zeta potential ( Fig. 1 L). Furthermore, RPM-SeNPs exhibited consistent effect on the cell viability to endothelial cells such as MAECs and HUVECs ( Fig. S1H–I ). Whereas the MAECs showed more efficient cellular internalization compared to HUVECs ( Fig. S1J ), and MAECs were considered as a cell model for subsequent mechanistic studies in consistent with the mice experiments.

A mouse model of PQ-induced vascular senescence ( Fig. 2 A) was established to evaluate the ameliorative effects of RPM-SeNPs. A significant body weight loss ( Fig. 2 B), accompanied by the senescence marker, as indicated by the positive SA-β-gal of aorta ( Fig. 2 C and D), higher expression of SASPS factors (p16, p21, p53, GMCSF, GROα, MCP-1, IL-1β, IL-8 and TNFα; Fig. 2 E–G), and higher protein levels of p21 ( Fig. 2 E–I). Although administration of RPM-SeNPs, RPM, or SeNPs mitigated body weight loss, aortic SA-β-gal activity, expression of SASP factors and p21 in mice with PQ exposure, and RPM-SeNPs exhibited a better effect. Accumulation of RPM-SeNPs was determined by labeling with C6 and RPM-SeNPs&C6 exhibited higher relative fluorescence intensity (RFI) in mouse aortas, livers and kidneys ( Fig. S2A–B ), as well as aortic, liver and kidney sections ( Fig. S2C–D ). Similarly, relatively higher Se levels were detected in aortas, liver, and kidney of mice treated with RPM-SeNPs compared to SeNPs ( Fig. S2E ). As a free radical generator, PQ induces vascular senescence mainly by activating oxidative stress. Consistent with this notion, higher levels of MDA (1.42-fold; Fig. 3 A), but lower levels of GSH (75.7 %; Fig. 3 B) were detected in the aortas of PQ-treated mice, which could be reversed by RPM-SeNP administration. For GPXs, a family of selenoenzymes responsible for antioxidant defense, lower activity (52.7 %; Fig. 3 C) along with reduced levels of mRNA (97.3 %, GPX1; 93.7 %, GPX4; Fig. 3 D) and protein (55.3 %, GPX1; 68.0 %, GPX4; Fig. 3 E and F) were detected in the aortas of PQ-treated mice, these were significantly ameliorated by administration of RPM-SeNPs or SeNPs. However, RPM-SeNPs significantly increased activity (94.4 % Fig. 3 C), mRNA (111.0 %, GPX1; 163.6 %, GPX4; Fig. 3 D), and protein (94.7 %, GPX1; 172.6 %, GPX4; Fig. 3 E and F) levels of GPXs. Similarly, higher RFI of GPX1 and GPX4 were observed in aortic sections from mice in PQ + RPM-SeNPs group compared to those of mice in PQ group ( Fig. 3 G–I). Notably, significant elevations of fluorescence intensity of GPX4 were observed in aortic endothelium of mice in PQ + RPM-SeNPs group ( Fig. 3 H and I). Sublethal H 2 O 2 was employed to induced endothelial senescence in MAECs and investigate the effects of RPM-SeNPs. H 2 O 2 treatment was found to induce a slight decrease in cell viability of MAECs within a short period of time ( Fig. S3A ). Interestingly, both RPM-SeNPs and SeNPs relieved cell viability reduction at Se concentrations below 2 μM, but RPM-SeNPs exhibited a relatively better effect ( Fig. S3B–C ). Based on these results, RPM-SeNPs (2 μM Se) was chosen for further study. RPM-SeNPs&C6 and SeNPs&C6 were taken up by MAECs in a short time, reaching a peak at about 6 h, with longer retention in cells at about 24 h. Notably, RPM-SeNPs&C6 were taken up more and faster into endothelial cells ( Fig. S3D–G ). Similar levels of intracellular Se concentration in cells were detected by HPLC-ICP-MS ( Fig. S3H ). Effects of RPM-SeNPs on endothelial senescence in MAECs were determined by SA-β-gal staining. Results showed that more SA-β-gal positive cells (77.7 %) were observed in the H 2 O 2 group compared with the control group, indicating oxidative stress induced endothelial senescence ( Fig. 4 A and B). Fewer SA-β-gal-stained cells were observed in the RPM-SeNPs, RPM, and SeNPs groups in comparison with the H 2 O 2 group, with RPM-SeNPs showing the most pronounced effect in reducing oxidative stress ( Fig. 4 A and B). Accordingly, the mRNA and protein levels of SASP (p16, p21, p53 and IL-1β) were elevated in H 2 O 2 group, while these were decreased in the H 2 O 2 +RPM-SeNPs group ( Fig. 4 C–F). Similar changes were observed in the MFI of p21 detected by immunofluorescence ( Fig. 4 G and H). Senescence in endothelial cells induced by H 2 O 2 led to dysfunction in migration and tube formation, and exhibited more adhesion to monocytes and these effects were ameliorated with RPM-SeNPs co-treatment ( Fig. S4A–F ). As expected, oxidative stress arose in senescent endothelial cells induced by H 2 O 2 , as indicated by overgeneration of ROS ( Fig. 5 A–D). Also, this led to increased levels of MDA ( Fig. 5 E) and decreased levels of GSH ( Fig. 5 F). In contrast, co-treatment with RPM-SeNPs diminished these effects. Similar to the results of mouse aortas, co-treatment with RPM-SeNPs significantly increased activity (204.5 %, Fig. 5 G), mRNA (90.7 %, Fig. 5 H) and protein (213.9 %, Fig. 5 I and J) levels of GPX4, as well as the MFI of GPX4 (157.6 %, Fig. 5 K and L) in senescent cells induced by H 2 O 2 . sections.discussion:
Oxidative stress-induced senescence of VECs triggers endothelial dysfunction, thereby facilitating the development and progression of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), including atherosclerosis, coronary artery disease, vascular calcification, hypertension, and stroke [ 1 , 3 ]. In this study, we set out to develop rapamycin coated Se nanoparticles (RPM-SeNPs) to investigate the synergistic effects of SeNPs and RPM in protecting against endothelial cell senescence. As expected, RPM-SeNPs exhibited an ameliorative effect on endothelial senescence in vivo and in vitro , by mitigating oxidative stress and activating mitophagy.

In consideration of the potential of Se supplementation for preventing or treating CVDs [ 32 , 50 ] and the promising therapeutic effects of RPM in delaying age-related pathologies [ 17 , 19 , 51 ], we investigated the potential of combining these two agents in the form of SeNPs and RPM-SeNPs. Spectral analysis revealed an effective interaction between RPM and SeNPs. UV–Vis spectroscopy showed a blue shift in the characteristic absorption peaks of both RPM and SeNPs, suggesting the formation of coordination or covalent bonds between the two components and confirming successful functionalization. FTIR spectroscopy further confirmed the successful functionalization of SeNPs with RPM. Key evidence includes characteristic absorption bands corresponding to RPM's core structure including the macrocyclic ring vibrations (C–H bending at 1455 cm −1 and symmetric C–H stretching at 2872 cm −1 ), the triene moiety (C <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" version="1.0" width="20.666667pt" height="16.000000pt" viewBox="0 0 20.666667 16.000000" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"><metadata> Created by potrace 1.16, written by Peter Selinger 2001-2019 </metadata><g transform="translate(1.000000,15.000000) scale(0.019444,-0.019444)" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"><path d="M0 440 l0 -40 480 0 480 0 0 40 0 40 -480 0 -480 0 0 -40z M0 280 l0 -40 480 0 480 0 0 40 0 40 -480 0 -480 0 0 -40z"/></g></svg> C stretching at 1634 cm −1 ), and the carbonyl group at 1720 cm −1 . Critically, the carbonyl peak exhibited a 4 cm −1 blue shift from 1720 cm −1 in free RPM to 1724 cm −1 in RPM-SeNPs, indicating electron density withdrawal from the C O bond due to coordination between carbonyl oxygen and surface Se atoms (C O–S chemisorption). Concurrently, the broadened and intensified O–H/N–H stretching band at 3424 cm −1 revealed hydrogen bonding interactions. This broadening signifies enhanced H-bond formation between the surface hydroxyl groups of SeNPs and the polar functional groups of RPM facilitating nanoparticle stabilization. These findings collectively confirm that RPM was successfully conjugated onto the surface of SeNPs via both covalent and non-covalent interactions, and resulting in the uniformly dispersed spherical morphology with higher stability, narrower size distribution and smaller particle size of RPM-SeNPs. RPM-SeNPs accumulated in mouse aortas without inducing hepatic or renal toxicity and were efficiently internalized by VECs. Interestingly, RPM was released more under intralysosomal mimic conditions than under physiological mimic conditions. This indicates that RPM is primarily released from RPM-SeNPs after cellular internalization, which allows for efficient delivery and utilization of RPM. Together, coating with RPM significantly optimizes SeNPs, resulting in a smaller size, higher stability, minimal toxicity, and superior bioavailability.

Despite forming a seemingly static monolayer in organs, the vascular endothelium acts as a highly dynamic and systemically distributed interactive organ, crucial for barrier maintenance, transport control, and blood pressure regulation. Direct exposure to oxidative stressors like ROS, inflammatory factors, and toxins makes endothelial cells susceptible to oxidative stress-induced premature senescence which also makes endothelial cells theoretically the most accessible targets for therapeutic intervention [ 52 ]. Both MAECs and HUVECs are widely used in studying endothelial aging, particularly in contexts involving oxidative stress, metabolic dysregulation, and inflammation, and share core senescence-related mechanisms like mTOR pathway activation. Although the both cells are available, MAECs are better model arterial functions, including vasodilation and ox-LDL uptake [ 53 , 54 ], while HUVECs are more commonly used in inflammation and angiogenesis studies [ 55 , 56 ]. To verify the effect of RPM-SeNPs on mitigating oxidative senescence of vascular endothelium, mice and MAECs were exposed to PQ and H 2 O 2 , respectively. As expected, RPM-SeNPs significantly mitigated endothelial senescence in vivo and in vitro , as evidenced by the relatively lower levels of SA-β-gal activity and SASP factors. Based on the calculated ratio of RPM to SeNPs in RPM-SeNPs of 1:120, the RPM dosage in RPM-SeNPs was approximately one-sixth of that in the RPM group. Notably, RPM-SeNPs exhibited a more potent anti-endothelial senescence activity than free RPM administered at a higher concentration both in vitro and in vivo , indicating that SeNPs-based delivery effectively enhances the biological efficacy of RPM in retarding cellular senescence. Endothelial senescence, which has been implicated in the development of CVDs, can largely explain endothelial dysfunction. Consistent with this notion, RPM-SeNPs exhibited a better mitigating effect on endothelial dysfunction in migration, tube formation and monocytes adhesion. These collective data suggest that SeNPs functionalized with RPM mitigate oxidative stress-induced senescence and endothelial dysfunction in endothelial cells. Cell cycle arrest, a hallmark of cellular senescence, is caused by the activation of the p53/p21 or p16/pRB pathway [ 57 ]. Although RPM-SeNPs downregulated the mRNA levels of p53, p21 and p16 in senescent endothelial cells, further investigation of RPM-SeNPs on cell cycle arrest, accompanied by inhibition of p53/p21 and p16/pRB pathways, is required.

Oxidative stress triggered by impaired redox homeostasis leads to premature senescence. Se and its metabolic species serve as potent antioxidants, exerting biological functions mainly via incorporation as selenocysteine into selenoproteins, including GPXs, thioredoxin reductases, selenoprotein K, selenoprotein R and selenoprotein W [ 58 ]. Consistent with the increased bioactivity of selenoprotein by SeNPs [ 45 ], RPM-SeNPs significantly increased the expressions of GPX1 and GPX4, the major GPXs responsible for anti-oxidative stress in endothelial cells and in mouse aortas. Our results showing that RPM-SeNPs significantly increased GPX4 in mouse aortic endothelium support the potent role of GPX4 in RPM-SeNPs in attenuating endothelial senescence. RPM-SeNPs also induced a significant upregulation of GPX4 in senescent MAECs, as well as GPX4 in ROS-generating mitochondria. Consistent with this finding, RPM-SeNPs alleviated redox imbalance in mouse aortas and MAECs as evidenced by the relatively lower levels of MDA and ROS (mtROS) coupled with higher levels of GSH and GPX activity. Notably, we observed a more pronounced fluctuation in mtGPX4 protein levels compared to cGPX4 during oxidative senescence. Specifically, H 2 O 2 challenge induced a more significant decrease of mtGPX4, while RPM-SeNPs treatment led to a stronger increase of mtGPX4 relative to cGPX4. This differential response indicates that mtGPX4 is particularly sensitive to the redox changes associated with aging. Subsequently, we found that the intervention of RPM-SeNPs to suppress key senescence markers was attenuated by siRNA-mediated depletion of mtGPX4, supporting a critical role for mtGPX4 in the protective effects of RPM-SeNPs against senescence. Taken together, these data suggest that RPM-SeNPs alleviate oxidative stress in senescent endothelial cells in large part by upregulating mtGPX4, particularly in dysfunctional mitochondria. In addition to mtGPX4, cGPX4 is translocated into mitochondria under stress through the translocase of outer membrane and translocase of the inner membrane complex [ 47 ]. However, the origin of increased GPX4 in dysfunctional mitochondria remains unclear and warrants further investigation. The present data is limited by lacking the mtGPX4 specific knockout models due to the mtGPX4 involving in multiple pathophysiological mechanisms, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis etc. To address this, further investigation of the origins and converging functions of mtGPX4 should be verified.

Mitophagy, the selective removal of dysfunctional or damaged mitochondria, is one of the most important mechanisms of mitochondrial quality control in cells [ 59 , 60 ]. Impairment of mitophagy is a feature of cellular senescence, whereas the reactivation of mitophagy by RPM is sufficient to reverse these changes. mTOR inhibits the activation of ULK1 and ULK1-mediated autophagy (mitophagy) by phosphorylating ULK1 at Ser757 and disrupting its interaction with AMPK, which can be inhibited by RPM [ 61 ]. In this study, RPM-SeNPs inhibited the activation of the PI3K (Y467/Y464/Y199)/Akt (Ser473)/mTOR (Ser2448)/ULK1 (Ser757) in senescent endothelial cells, suggesting the positive effects of RPM-SeNPs on autophagy. Additionally, RPM-SeNPs significantly boosted colocalization of lysosomes with mitochondria accompanied by elevated levels of Beclin1, p62, LC3BII/LC3BI ratio, and LC3B/mitochondria colocalization. This further supports the activation of mitophagy in the presence of RPM-SeNPs. Impairment of selective clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria leads to excessive mtROS generation, reduced ATP generation, decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, and downregulated transcript levels of mtDNA, which were significantly alleviated by RPM-SeNPs. This suggests that the activation of mitophagy by RPM-SeNPs effectively restores mitochondrial function. Mitochondrial GPX4 (mtGPX4 and translocated cGPX4) is mainly degraded during mitophagy [ 47 ] , which in turn amplifies oxidative stress and causes oxidation of Atg3 and Atg7 [ 48 ] and reverses inhibition of mitophagy. Although RPM-SeNPs elevated GPX4 in dysfunctional mitochondria, whether this is achieved by inhibiting GPX4 degradation and promotes mitophagy by inhibiting Atg3 and Atg7 oxidation was not determined.
sections.conclusion: In this study, we successfully developed RPM-SeNPs with a molar ratio of RPM to SeNPs of 1:120, exhibiting smaller size, higher uniformity and increased bioavailability. RPM-SeNPs effectively alleviated oxidative stress-induced senescence in vascular endothelium by enhancing antioxidant defenses through the upregulation of GPX4, this effect particularly involved mtGPX4, thereby demonstrating significant antioxidant capacity. Moreover, RPM-SeNPs promote mitophagy by inhibiting the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway, which helps to mitigate mitochondrial dysfunction caused by oxidative stress and ultimately protects cellular integrity and function. Overall, these findings offer novel insights into the anti-aging efficacy of RPM-SeNPs in mitigating oxidative stress-induced endothelial senescence and its associated CVDs.
